items.author: 0xAsm0d3us

items.content:
some alpha drop for doing inexpensive vuln research. 

instead of writing an article on the prompts/process behind this bounty (and more), I am dropping some prompts and the thought process I used as part of this research.

ik you might say prompts don't matter much, frontier models' baseline intelligence can rawdog vuln discovery (and it is true to a good extent), but there is a high chance that you either do not have access to cyber models, or even if you do, they are expensive (and with heavy guardrails). The idea is, these prompts work well with open-weight/less expensive models. Not saying these will outperform the raw intelligence and capabilities of frontier models, but open-weight models perform much better with a bounded/goal-specific approach (where the goal is set, and the search space is massive) rather than open-ended exploration (where the goal is vague, and the search space is massive).

anyway, here are some prompts. I don't need to share much, because you can just create variations of these and apply them wherever you wish.

- find places where the app is supposed to enforce something, but doesn't actually enforce it.

- find security rules that are enforced in one part of the app, but just assumed to be true in another.

- find security assumptions the app relies on, but never actually checks or enforces.

- find places where the app depends on undocumented behavior, and what happens if that behavior changes.

- find operations that are secure on their own, but become vulnerable when you combine or chain them together.

- find cases where the same object can be accessed in different ways, but each way ends up having different permissions.

- find objects whose identity can be changed or rebound to another user, without going through the right checks.

- find requests that get rejected or fail, but still end up changing something or triggering a side effect.

- find security checks that only work if certain events happen in a specific order, and what happens if that order changes.

- find operations where the transaction fails or rolls back, but some of the side effects still happen.

- find things you can still do with an object even after it has been deleted, or access to it has been revoked.

- find state changes that can be reversed or undone by someone who shouldn't have permission to do so.

- find objects that can end up in two contradictory states at the same time, and what operations become possible because of that.

I take such prompts, put it in a mutator (which has threat model of the project I am doing sec engagement), the mutator will mutate the prompts based on the threat model, and spawn swarm of agents, with different starting prompt and a bounded goal, the process repeats till all paths are exhauted, or some new signal is generated, which then feeds back to mutator. 

Doing this using a cheap model is very effective and sometimes it might yield you something even expensive models miss, we are just trying to maxximise the search space, from as many angles as possible, and once this process generates enough signals, just use a frontier model to confirm/triage issues, or for finding similar variants of such issues, that's basically it. There is v less moat is making a custom harness (unless you are an elite vuln research who can codify their approach in it or a 100x agentic engineer, I am neither).

items.content:
RT @qwerty__cs: Google DeepMind's AI agents found two new weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA, in just a few weeks.

Working under human guidance with cryptanalysis experts from UC San Diego and Inria, the agents came up with:
• A signature forgery method that, when the attacker controls only a small part of the signed data such as a 32-byte digest, is in theory about 1,600x faster than the previous best for 1024-bit keys
• A batch factoring method that cuts the cost of each additional 1024-bit key by about 30x compared with earlier batch techniques

RSA-2048 and larger keys aren't affected, so banking, messaging and software updates are fine. The ones exposed are older systems still running 1024-bit keys.

items.content:
RT @zacker150: Actual software engineer here.

Vibe coding is when you use AI to write software without manually reviewing every single line of code. Instead, you rely on empirical tests, formal verification, and static analysis to verify that your code is correct.

Rewrites like the Discord rewrite are prime targets for vibe coding because you can easily verify them. Just take the old code, run it with a ton of random inputs (this is called fuzzing), and compare the output with the new code. Your rewrite is done when the output is always the same. 

As for how you know it's vibe coded? Everything is vibe coded these days. Software engineers don't write code by hand anymore. Instead, we herd clankers writing code.

items.content:
RT @Kostastsale: We captured this attack as well, and managed to follow the execution chain quite a bit further.

It started with the same obfuscated PowerShell command using curl.exe and a decimal-encoded IP (𝟷𝟹𝟼𝟿𝟿𝟾𝟶𝟺𝟼𝟷 → 𝟾𝟷.𝟷𝟼𝟾.𝟼𝟸.𝟺𝟻). From there, we observed multiple stages of payload delivery, persistence, process injection, and credential access.

Here's what we saw:

1️⃣ PowerShell downloaded 𝚏𝚕𝚘𝚖𝚘𝚘𝚏𝟷.𝚣𝚒𝚙 from 𝚖𝚊𝚒𝚕𝚍𝚎𝚟𝚎𝚕𝚘𝚙𝚎𝚛.𝚜𝚒𝚝𝚎, extracted it under AppData\Local\ExFiles, and executed 𝚏𝚕𝚘𝚖𝚘.𝚎𝚡𝚎.
2️⃣ flomo.exe established persistence through the user Run key (𝚎𝚕𝚎𝚌𝚝𝚛𝚘𝚗.𝚊𝚙𝚙.𝚏𝚕𝚘𝚖𝚘), then extracted and launched 𝚄𝚝𝚒𝚕𝚒𝚝𝚢𝙿𝚒𝚡𝚎.𝚎𝚡𝚎.
3️⃣ UtilityPixe.exe copied itself to 𝙲:\𝙿𝚛𝚘𝚐𝚛𝚊𝚖𝙳𝚊𝚝𝚊\𝚑𝚊𝚗𝚍𝚕𝚎𝚛_𝚍𝚋𝚐_𝚍𝚎𝚟\ and staged a legacy scheduled task file (JSONGateway_debug.job).
4️⃣ It then spawned XenoMixe.exe suspended and modified its thread context using 𝚆𝚘𝚠𝟼𝟺𝚂𝚎𝚝𝚃𝚑𝚛𝚎𝚊𝚍𝙲𝚘𝚗𝚝𝚎𝚡𝚝.
5️⃣ 𝚇𝚎𝚗𝚘𝙼𝚒𝚡𝚎.𝚎𝚡𝚎 accessed Edge's Cookies, Local State, and Login Data files, registered raw keyboard input hooks, and injected into an active Edge process using SetThreadContext.
6️⃣ Browser data was staged into temporary directories and .7z archives. We also observed AD reconnaissance using net group "domain computers" /dom.
7️⃣ Network activity included 𝚐𝚙𝚝𝚌𝚖𝚍.𝚒𝚘 and outbound connections to multiple IPs on ports 2222/2223.

One thing worth noting is that we confirmed access to browser credential stores and data staging, but couldn't verify successful exfiltration from the available network telemetry.

IOCs:
𝟺𝟻[.]𝟷𝟹𝟷[.]𝟸𝟷𝟺[.]𝟸𝟹𝟿:𝟸𝟸𝟸𝟸 ➔  attempted a TCP connection from 𝚇𝚎𝚗𝚘𝙼𝚒𝚡𝚎.𝚎𝚡𝚎

𝟾𝟺[.]𝟸𝟻𝟸[.]𝟼𝟼[.]𝟷𝟽𝟼  ➔ XenoMixe.exe attempted TCP connections on ports 2222 and 2223

𝚐𝚙𝚝𝚌𝚖𝚍[.]𝚒𝚘 ➔  Resolved by the injected malware process 𝚇𝚎𝚗𝚘𝙼𝚒𝚡𝚎.𝚎𝚡𝚎 to establish bidirectional network communication on TCP ports 3333 and 3334, operating as C2.

𝚖𝚊𝚒𝚕𝚍𝚎𝚟𝚎𝚕𝚘𝚙𝚎𝚛[.]𝚜𝚒𝚝𝚎 ➔ Repeatedly resolved by a staging executable (flomo.exe) and served as the source for downloading malicious payloads during staging of additional components.

𝚑𝚝𝚝𝚙://𝟾𝟷\[.]𝟷𝟼𝟾\[.]𝟼𝟸\[.]𝟺𝟻/𝚓𝚎𝚜𝚜/𝚊𝚙𝚒?𝚝=<𝚄𝙸𝙳>&𝚝𝚛𝚊𝚌𝚔=𝟷&𝚎𝚟𝚎𝚗𝚝=𝚍𝚕_𝚘𝚔
